_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Studies link supportive childhoods and father involvement to well-being
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A study led by the University of Nottingham found that adults in the United Kingdom, United States and Japan who recalled more supportive childhood experiences reported better health, greater happiness and life satisfaction and lower anxiety [scitechdaily.com#1]. More supportive childhood experiences were also associated with stronger social connections, a greater sense of neighborhood belonging and more trust in others. The study, published Sept. 30 in the Journal of Happiness Studies, surveyed adults ages 18 to 34 [scitechdaily.com#1]. The findings show associations, not proof that childhood experiences caused adult outcomes: participants recalled their upbringing and reported their current well-being [scitechdaily.com#1]. Separately, a review of fatherhood research described links between sustained positive father involvement and children’s cognitive, social and emotional outcomes, while noting that the findings were correlational [time.com#1].

items.title: [phys.org] Forensic study finds signs of sacrifice in ancient Egyptian royal burials
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A forensic re-examination of 46 skulls excavated near First Dynasty royal tombs at Umm el-Qaab, Egypt, identified potentially fatal injuries in 18, strengthening the case that some people buried there were killed as retainers after a ruler’s death [sciencealert.com#1][theguardian.com#1][thenationalnews.com#1]. The skulls came from burials around the tombs of King Djer, King Djet and Queen Merneith; many graves were associated with royal officials and artisans [theguardian.com#1][skai.gr#1]. British Egyptologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s and suspected retainer sacrifice, but could not identify fatal injuries. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University interpreted the newly identified trauma as evidence that at least some people died violently, but stressed that the sample is small and cannot establish what happened to everyone buried there [theguardian.com#1][arstechnica.com#1]. Petrie reburied most of the remains, and Campbell said she would like to locate and analyze them [popsci.com#1][sciencealert.com#1].

items.title: [ArchDaily] Building and Unbuilding: An Approach to Circular Timber Construction Addressing Material Waste
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

In the face of the climate crisis and within the framework of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, the reuse of materials has become prominent in the fields of construction and architecture in recent years. From "urban mining" to life cycle assessments (LCAs), professionals, organizations, and researchers are exploring different solutions and strategies to address the same overarching challenge. Project (Un)Build is a research initiative developing reversible timber construction methods that use straps and friction pads to facilitate material reuse. It contributes to the ongoing debate and reflection on the act of building itself.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Jingzhou City Wall Archaeological Site Exhibition Pavilion / Qing Studio
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A Millennium Cross-Section on a Living Street — This project originates from a major breakthrough in the archaeological discovery and conservation practice at Bastion No. 11 of the Jingzhou City Wall. Since 2016, this section of the ancient wall had been listed for emergency conservation due to foundation settlement and structural cracking. During the repair process, a stratified structure of "walls built upon walls," spanning the Five Dynasties, Song, Ming, and Qing periods, was uncovered. This led to the approval by the National Cultural Heritage Administration for systematic archaeological excavation.
